ai.definition: Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) elimination refers to the process of reducing the incidence and prevalence of NTDs, such as lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, and river blindness, to levels that are no longer considered public health problems. This is achieved through mass drug administration (MDA), vector control measures, and disease surveillance.
ai.howItWorks: NTD elimination programs involve the widespread distribution of antiparasitic drugs to at-risk populations to prevent infection. Vector control measures such as insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor residual spraying are used to reduce transmission. Surveillance systems track disease prevalence and monitor program effectiveness.
ai.problemSolved: Eliminating NTDs addresses health disparities, improves quality of life, and reduces economic burden in affected communities by preventing chronic illness and disability.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves producing antiparasitic drugs on a large scale. Vector control devices like bed nets are mass-produced using textile manufacturing processes.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes drug formulation, packaging, and distribution logistics for MDA programs. For vector control, it involves fabricating and distributing bed nets and other equipment.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include drug production costs, distribution logistics, training of health workers, and ongoing surveillance efforts. Vector control measures also incur significant costs related to the distribution and maintenance of devices.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as several NTDs have been eliminated in individual countries, but widespread global elimination remains a challenge due to resource constraints and varying disease prevalence.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but generally require adherence to international guidelines for drug distribution and vector control. WHO provides guidance on best practices.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for drug resistance, challenges in reaching remote or underserved populations, and the need for sustained funding and political commitment.
ai.profitability: Profitability is not a primary focus as these programs are often funded by international organizations and NGOs. However, successful elimination can lead to long-term economic benefits through improved workforce productivity and reduced healthcare costs.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include the introduction of new drugs, improved vector control technologies, and more integrated approaches combining multiple NTD interventions.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Surveillance systems require minimal power for data collection but can be battery-operated in remote areas.

glossary.def: A group of tropical diseases that are primarily found in resource-poor settings and have a significant impact on public health.
The large-scale distribution of antiparasitic drugs to at-risk populations to prevent infection with NTDs.
Strategies to reduce the population of disease-carrying insects, such as mosquitoes and flies, which transmit NTDs.

subsystems.name: Preventive chemotherapy drugs
subsystems.role: single-dose tablets that clear or suppress parasites in whole populations without individual diagnosis.

subsystems.name: Drug manufacture and supply
subsystems.role: produce tablets at the millions-of-doses scale a national campaign needs.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics and mapping
subsystems.role: find where the disease still circulates and decide when to stop treating.

subsystems.name: Vector and intermediate-host control
subsystems.role: block transmission by attacking the insects and snails that carry the parasite.

subsystems.name: Community delivery
subsystems.role: get tablets to everyone at risk, often where there are few clinics.

subsystems.name: Surveillance and verification
subsystems.role: prove elimination holds and detect any rebound.
parts: mosquito and snail testing for parasite DNA

buildSteps.title: Map the burden
buildSteps.detail: Surveys establish which districts are endemic and how intense transmission is, so treatment is targeted rather than blanket.

buildSteps.title: Secure the drugs
buildSteps.detail: National programmes draw on donated or low-cost tablets and forecast the number of doses needed district by district.

buildSteps.title: Recruit and train distributors
buildSteps.detail: Community health workers and volunteers are trained to dose by weight or height, record who was treated and manage side effects.

buildSteps.title: Run mass treatment rounds
buildSteps.detail: Whole at-risk populations are dosed annually or twice-yearly, aiming to treat at least 65% of them, until transmission falls below a threshold.

buildSteps.title: Add vector control
buildSteps.detail: Nets, spraying or snail control are layered on where drugs alone will not interrupt transmission.

buildSteps.title: Monitor coverage and impact
buildSteps.detail: Coverage surveys and repeated infection surveys show whether rounds are working.

buildSteps.title: Assess whether to stop
buildSteps.detail: Transmission assessment surveys in children test whether new infections have stopped; passing them allows treatment to be halted.

buildSteps.title: Switch to surveillance
buildSteps.detail: After treatment stops, the programme keeps testing people, mosquitoes or snails so any resurgence is caught early.

buildSteps.title: Verify elimination
buildSteps.detail: A national dossier is reviewed externally, and the country is certified free of transmission as a public health problem.

prerequisites.tech: Drugs safe enough to give whole populations without diagnosis
prerequisites.why: mass treatment only works if the medicine is cheap, single-dose and has very low risk of harm.
programmes need to measure infection in remote villages without laboratories.
for vector-borne NTDs, drugs alone often cannot break transmission.
most current medicines kill larvae; adult worms survive and restart transmission, so many years of rounds are needed.
there is no licensed vaccine for most of these diseases, so control rests on drugs and vectors.

pathway.milestone: national mass-treatment programmes reaching around a billion people a year in over 100 countries
pathway.unlocks: sharp falls in infection in many districts, and in some countries elimination.

pathway.milestone: countries finishing the last treatment rounds and passing transmission assessment
pathway.unlocks: verified elimination status, as achieved for trachoma in Ghana in 2018 and lymphatic filariasis in Sri Lanka in 2016, and a shift of budgets to surveillance.

pathway.milestone: new regimens and tools for the hardest settings, including triple-drug therapy for lymphatic filariasis and safer options where ivermectin cannot be used
pathway.unlocks: faster interruption of transmission in conflict zones and co-endemic areas.

pathway.milestone: post-elimination surveillance sustained across whole regions
pathway.unlocks: keeping diseases from returning and freeing health systems for other work.
